title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, one Goddess in nine forms. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Did you keep going at one thing you wanted to drop? Day six hundred eighty.

In North India, Diwali is usually a night: the lamps come out after dark, for Rama coming home. In Tamil Nadu, a family's Deepavali can begin around four in the morning. Someone wakes the house while it's still pitch dark. Each person sits down, and an elder rubs warm sesame oil into their hair. Then a hot bath, new clothes, a firecracker before sunrise, sweets for breakfast. Same festival name. Different hour, different story. This one isn't about Rama at all.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `WARM OIL, A HOT BATH, NEW CLOTHES.` → `A DIFFERENT STORY.`

segments.voice: The story belongs to Krishna and a demon king named Naraka. The Bhagavata Purana tells it. Naraka has grown arrogant and cruel. He has stolen treasures from the gods, among them the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and he holds thousands of young women captive in his fortress city. Krishna flies there on Garuda, with his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks through the fortress walls, and kills Naraka in battle. Then two things happen that are easy to skip and worth noticing. The Earth herself, Naraka's mother in the story, comes forward, returns the stolen treasures, and asks Krishna to protect Naraka's son. And Krishna goes into the fortress and frees the women, sixteen thousand of them in the Bhagavata's count, and takes them under his protection so none is shamed. Many families tell a further detail: that Naraka, dying, asked that the day of his death be remembered with lights. That's the day before the main Diwali night, called Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Naraka. In much of South India, it is Deepavali, kept before dawn. The oil bath, people say, recalls Krishna bathing after the battle. So the row of lamps has more than one road leading to it. In Ayodhya's story, the lamps guide a king home. In this one, a fortress is broken open and thousands of women walk out, free, toward home. Both versions light the way out of the dark.
screen: `NARAKA: A CRUEL KING, A FORTRESS.` · `KRISHNA AND SATYABHAMA ON GARUDA.` · `THE CAPTIVES WALK FREE.` · `NARAKA CHATURDASHI: BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ONE ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: If you can, light one small light, or simply picture one. Sit with it and let the breath slow. This time, think of someone who is stuck somewhere: in a hard job, an illness, a lonely stretch, a place they can't leave. Picture your small light at the door of that place, showing a way out. Hold them and the light together, without needing to fix anything. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. In much of the South, Deepavali comes before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi, remembering Krishna's victory and the captives set free.
Your line: light the way home. Today, do one small thing that helps someone get out of a tight spot: a ride, an introduction, a word. Day six hundred eighty.

original.note: Sanskrit naraka (the king's name) + caturdaśī (the fourteenth lunar day): the day before the main Diwali night.

trapdoor: what you thought: Diwali is about Rama, everywhere.
what it means: in much of the South, it's about Krishna defeating Naraka and freeing his captives, kept before dawn.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book tells Naraka's defeat; the oil bath and Naraka's dying wish are popular explanations attached to the festival.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.59 (Krishna and Satyabhama defeat Naraka; the captives freed)

notes: Confirm Bhagavata 10.59 details: Satyabhama accompanies Krishna on Garuda; the Earth (Bhumi) returns Aditi's earrings and asks protection for Naraka's son Bhagadatta; the number of captives (16,000 or 16,100 by reading).
In some tellings Satyabhama herself kills Naraka; the script follows the Bhagavata where Krishna does.
Naraka's dying wish and the oil bath's link to Krishna are popular explanations; marked as 'many families tell' and 'people say'.
Krishna's marriage to the freed women is not mentioned; a Keeper may want it.
